comments.text:
For my dollar i'm still holding off on any RTX cards until there are a heaping handful of compelling and BRAND NEW (i.e. not Quake 2) reasons to buy one of these cards.  My 1070ti still sits pretty for all my 1080p needs and will probably continue to do so for another couple years.

What i predict will happen that will finally bring more games into the RTX era is actually the next generation of game consoles.  A developer knowing that there are currently just a tiny bit more than 3% of steam users (source - steam hardware survey June 2019) that can turn on RTX has got to be very demotivating to even offer the tech in their games.... but if they were to know that the minor pc RT-capable base AND the console install base could enjoy the benefits -- that will get development studios on board.

If the console manufacturers weren't going to include RT capable hardware in their next consoles, i would say without doubt that the tech would die much the same way Physx died - with a tiny handful of pointless improvements in a small number of games that had almost no impact on the overall gameplay experience.  

Truth be told, half the time i feel that way about RT now vs. the finely tuned, well-weathered methods used in games currently.  I'm ready to be convinced that this future is the one we should all look forward to.

Yeah, that also makes perfect sense in English...  These comments say "Nobody said nothing."  In English that literally means "Everyone said something."


The comments are formatted as follows (once more...)


No One:

This does not say "Nobody said anything."


The speaker being "No One" in this instance means there is no person saying what was about to be written.  By writing nothing at all you are stating that nothing was said.  So you are saying that "no speaker said: no words."

No matter what native language you may speak, it doesn't make the comment any less incorrect.  That isn't how English works, it's written in English, it's wrong in English.

comments.text:
Whomever buys these is going to be Super annoyed when they realize they are Super owned by 7nm refresh next year (+50% faster, node dropping from 12 to 7nm). Those saying that "yeah but every year something faster comes out", sure, valid point, but unlike mid-cycle refreshes of yore where the only refresh was the 80 Ti card which was 30%+ faster than the 80 card for the same price (GTX 1080 MSRP at launch) this is pretty much a slap in the face at 7% faster. To add insult to injury is the fact that this is how fast these cards should have been at launch (historically, the incoming 70 card has always been as fast as the outgoing 80 Ti card, not 10% slower). I'm still of the belief that they renamed the entire Turing launch one GPU higher, i.e. "RTX 2070", with a 60 card SKU, TU-106, no SLI, only as fast as the outgoing 80 card, the "2080 Ti", only 25-30% faster than the outgoing 80 Ti card (where the incoming 80 card historically is). Basically, NGreedia doubled the prices if you look at it this way: 



RTX "2070", in actuality a $600 60 card. 
RTX "2080", in actuality a $900 70 card. 
RTX "2080 Ti", in actuality a $1200 before taxes (those taxes scale something fierce, this is $1350 card out the door) 80 card. 


And now mid-cycle, they release variants that are as fast as they should have been from the get-go only because AMD released an alternative and they expect morons to line up in droves for this knowing full well that everyone is going to be mighty upset come Q2-Q4 2020 when they release architecture on the 7nm mode. 


We aren't talking about a refinement of a node (Pascal to Maxwell, both 12nm) we are talking about an exponential drop in node size. 


If you buy Super, youre going to Super regret it.


Also, why is NGreedia so stingy with the VRAM to begin with? Marketing tactic? Just put 12GB on everything, GDDR6 isn't expensive HBM2 for crying out loud. For $400 for the 60 card that thing should have 12GG of video memory. Hell the 980M from 2014 in my laptop has 8GB of video memory (Desktop: 8700k @ 5.0 GHz + 1080 Ti)!

comments.text:
Anchoring effect in action! "These cards appear to be a pretty great value for the consumer", compared to the predecessors, yes. Compared to what we were used to a number years ago, no! 


I've argued in the past that Nvidia is somewhat justified in their prices for these huge chips (TU102 @ 754 mm^2), but justification for the prices doesn't equal good value for the consumer. Real-time ray tracing IS the future, but that doesn't mean everyone wants to pay for it at this moment in time. The top-of-the-range GeForce GTX 280's GT200 was a massive chip for its time (the largest TSMC had ever produced) at 576 mm^2, but that card launched for £449, with Trusted Reviews calling that "astronomical" at the time, yet in today's money accounting for inflation (average of 2.6% per year here in the UK) that is still only £552. So I wouldn't call the 2080 (with a 545 mm^2 die) coming in at £669 a pretty great value when it's 21% more expensive than a GPU described in 2011 as astronomical in price. Not to mention that the 280 was the highest-end card, whilst the 2080 is not (although their die sizes are comparable with the extra space needed for RT and Tensor cores).


The elephant in the room however, is ballooning costs as we go to smaller process nodes, which is partly to blame for ballooning card prices. That and little competition in the market for the last few years! AMD seems to be on the right track to get around these spiralling costs per mm^2 by using chiplets to raise effective product yield with Zen. Hopefully we will see GPU design finally make the jump to chiplets in the not-too-distant future and enable prices to come back down to sane levels!
